children.text: Key Takeaways
A helmet’s inner foam liner compresses permanently after absorbing impact and cannot be restored.
Visible damage to the outer shell does not confirm or rule out liner compression.
Any crash while wearing a helmet is reason enough to replace it, regardless of how minor the impact seemed.
Helmets degrade from heat, UV exposure, and hair products and should be replaced every five to seven years.
DOT and Snell certifications confirm a helmet was tested against real crash forces, not just marketed as protective gear.

Motorcycle riders face serious risks on Denver roads, and a helmet is one of the few things standing between a rider and a traumatic brain injury. What many riders do not realize is that a helmet’s protective ability ends the moment its inner liner absorbs an impact. You should
replace the helmet after a fall
, even if it looks undamaged on the outside. At
Dormer Harpring
, our
motorcycle accident lawyer
represents motorcycle accident victims in Denver who suffered head injuries after crashes, sometimes worsened by a
defective helmet
, and we understand how equipment failure and rider choices affect outcomes when lives are on the line.
How Do Helmets Work?

Helmets are designed with two key components that make them effective at protecting the head and skull from external forces that could cause injury: a hard outer shell and a soft inner liner. The hard shell that comprises the exterior of a helmet is designed to resist impact and prevent penetration. It is the first line of defense in an accident.

The inner liner is usually made from some type of foam or material that is soft enough to absorb the force of an impact but durable enough to protect the skull. The purpose of the inner liner is to compress or deform upon impact, allowing it to absorb energy and spread it out to reduce the amount of force transmitted to the wearer’s head.
Can I Use a Helmet After It’s Been Dropped? – Dropping a motorcycle helmet

If a helmet is dropped with enough force to compress the inner liner, it should be replaced. The crushing of the foam liner cannot be reversed. Most helmets use expanded polystyrene (EPS) inner liners, which consist of plastic beads packed together with air bubbles. Upon impact (even a minor impact), these air bubbles can get squished and will not be able to regain their position. Dropping a motorcycle helmet, even from a short height, can compromise its ability to properly absorb a second or subsequent impact.

If the helmet was not dropped with enough force to crush the inner liner, its energy absorption properties most likely would not have been damaged. However, if an impact to a helmet is severe enough to affect the inner liner and crush the air bubbles in the EPS, it will no longer perform up to the
Snell Memorial Foundation’s safety standards
. The liner’s ability to manage, reduce and dissipate impact forces will be adversely affected in this deformed condition and the helmet must be replaced.
Why Should I Replace My Helmet After a Motorcycle Accident?
A crash puts forces on a helmet that a simple drop does not. The same kind of head-first impacts that cause serious
trampoline injuries

can hit a rider in a collision, and when a helmet absorbs that impact while on your head, the liner compresses from the inside out, under the full weight and momentum of a collision. That level of stress goes well beyond what a drop produces, and the damage left behind is just as invisible.

No crack, scratch, or dent on the outer shell will tell you whether the foam inside has already given way. The exterior can look completely intact while the liner has been permanently compromised. Riders who hold onto a helmet after a crash are betting their safety on a component that may have already done its job and has nothing left to give.
Once a helmet has been worn through any accident, the only safe decision is to
replace the helmet

and start over with one whose protection you can actually count on. The stakes make the choice straightforward. A new helmet costs far less than the medical bills that follow a second head injury, and the absence of visible damage is never proof that the helmet is still performing at full capacity.
When to Replace Your Helmet
Knowing when to retire a helmet does not require a technical inspection. The situations below each call for immediate replacement:
After any crash or impact while wearing it, replace the helmet. The liner absorbed energy during that event and cannot guarantee full protection in a second impact, regardless of visible damage.
After a significant drop while empty, evaluate the helmet carefully. A drop from handlebar height or higher warrants replacement, even if the shell shows no damage.
After five to seven years of regular use, replace the helmet regardless of condition. Heat, UV exposure, and hair products degrade foam and shell materials over time.
When the fit changes, stop riding with it. A helmet that once felt snug and no longer does has likely experienced internal material breakdown.
After purchasing used, buy new instead. There is no reliable way to verify a secondhand helmet’s impact history.

If any of these situations apply, replace the helmet. Assuming a used or post-impact helmet is still functional is a risk no rider should take. That principle carries into the next decision every rider eventually faces: choosing a replacement that actually meets the demands of Denver riding.
Choosing the Right Motorcycle Helmet

Choosing the right motorcycle helmet in Denver means prioritizing DOT or Snell safety certifications, matching your head shape to a snug-fitting helmet, and selecting a style suited to Denver’s varied riding conditions.
Three things matter most in a replacement helmet:
Certification:
According to the
National Highway Traffic Safety Administration

, look for a DOT label on the back, which confirms the helmet meets Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard No. 218. A Snell certification means it has passed additional independent impact testing. A helmet carrying neither label has not been verified to protect you in a crash.
Fit:

Head shapes generally fall into three categories: oval, intermediate oval, and round oval. A helmet that fits correctly sits level on the head, makes full contact with the crown, and does not shift when pushed side to side. As the
CDC
notes, a poor fit significantly reduces the protection a certified helmet can provide.
Style:

Full-face helmets offer the most coverage and work best for highway riding on routes like I-25 and I-70. Modular helmets have a chin bar that lifts for city riding while still providing full coverage when closed.

The right helmet reduces the risk of serious injury, but when a crash occurs due to someone else’s negligence on Denver roads, understanding your legal options matters just as much as the gear you were wearing.
